item.title: Susie Wiles' old lobbying firm in crosshairs of MAGA feud
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
For the last two years, Brian Ballard's ties to President Trump made his lobbying firm one of the most sought-after in Washington. Now those same ties have made it a target in the Republican Party's post-midterm infighting. Calley Means, a former top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., alleged in an interview Sunday with CBS News' "Face the Nation" that Ballard Partners "controlled" White House policy. Mr. Trump's former chief of staff , Susie Wiles, worked at the firm for nearly a decade as a managing partner, leaving in 2019. Means claimed Ballard Partners' rise to become the top-earning lobbying firm "did not happen by accident." He accused Wiles and other top advisers to Mr. Trump of catering to industries that funded Republicans ahead of the midterms. Ballard and Wiles both called the claims false. The firm's interactions with Wiles as chief of staff "have been limited and have been the exception, not the rule," Brian Ballard, a longtime Trump fundraiser, said in a rare statement Sunday. Ballard Partners' more than $88 million in lobbying revenue last year was, at the time, the most any firm had reported since the Lobbying Disclosure Act took effect in 1996, even after adjusting for inflation, a CBS News analysis of Senate lobbying disclosures found. Through the first three quarters of 2026, the firm has already surpassed that, reporting more than $98 million. The fortunes of Washington lobbying firms tend to rise and fall with changes in administrations, as companies hire them to try to influence policy. But after an election that saw government corruption polling as a top issue for voters, questions about who has profited from political connections are intensifying. Ballard Partners is now among those ensnared in the MAGA feud. That tension could deepen ahead of 2028, as Republicans who cheered Mr. Trump's promise to "drain the swamp" speak out about the realities of an entrenched lobbying industry that has continued to thrive in Washington. "The Democrats are going to start investigations as soon as they're sworn in, and White House fighting about who was making money will just elevate the topic," said Marc Short, a former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence. The White House said in a statement that the Trump administration "has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions." A fight over vapes Brian Ballard has been one of Mr. Trump's top fundraisers for years, having reeled in $50 million for his campaign in 2024, according to a source familiar with the number who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Since 2008, he has chaired Florida finance committees for previous Republican presidential nominees. His firm opened a Washington office in 2017 and once employed both Wiles and Pam Bondi, who went on to serve as Mr. Trump's attorney general. When Mr. Trump won a second term, the firm signed up hundreds of clients, though its relationship with the administration has seen ups and downs. For a brief period in 2025, Brian Ballard was banned from the West Wing after his firm's lobbying approach for a cryptocurrency client frustrated White House officials, two Trump advisers told CBS News. (Ballard apologized in May 2025 and returned to the White House's good graces, Axios reported .) Among the firm's longest-standing clients is RAI Services Company, a subsidiary of tobacco giant Reynolds American. It has paid Ballard Partners millions of dollars since 2017, lobbying records show. That relationship placed Ballard at the center of Means' allegations about favorable treatment for vaping interests. Means resigned in late October, claiming the Make America Healthy Again agenda had stalled in the White House. He placed the blame at Wiles' feet, saying she and "her deputies were still relentlessly pushing HHS to find a pathway for fruit-flavored vapes." In May, the Food and Drug Administration handed the tobacco industry a win with new guidance that could let major tobacco companies sell flavored vapes. The announcement came a week after Brian Ballard and tobacco executives had lunch with Mr. Trump at his golf club in Jupiter, Florida, where the president called Kennedy and other health officials to complain about the FDA, The New York Times reported . The FDA decision also came after RAI Services Company had given $5 million to MAGA Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC, on April 30, Federal Election Commission records show . (FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned days after the guidance came out, in protest .) The White House has suggested the donation had nothing to do with the FDA decision. In his statement Sunday, Ballard said no one at his firm advocated to Wiles or anyone at the White House on authorization for fruit-flavored vapes. He said his advocacy related to "illegal, unregulated vapes from China," some of which, he said, have been found to be laced with fentanyl. Wiles told CBS News she had nothing to do with the tobacco industry meeting with Mr. Trump at his golf club. Means also singled out James Blair, the former deputy chief of staff, claiming he was "relentless on helping the fruit-flavored vape industry." Blair, who left the White House in April to oversee the GOP's midterm strategy, has traded barbs with Means on social media, calling the claim that he pushed vapes as a core midterm issue "a complete and total lie." "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair told CBS News, adding that he was tasked with making sure the FDA ruled on nicotine product applications swiftly – within six months. "Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely," Blair added. Blair spoke with Reynolds and other vape companies about the FDA's application process, but not about any specific applications or products, according to two sources familiar with the conversations who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Blair has said he is reviewing his legal options and whether to sue Means for defamation. A MAGA Inc. spokesperson said the group "is pleased to accept legal contributions from those who agree with President Trump's America First agenda." A spokesperson for Wiles told Axios that Means' accusations of corruption were "outrageous, defamatory, and provably false." "What Ballard helps you do" Means' accusations centered on what he called a "very close-knit crew" around Wiles that "explicitly catered to special interests." He alleged that the goal was to serve big business interests in exchange for money for the midterms. Steering those donations, he alleged, "is what Ballard helps you do." Lobbying firms in Washington routinely advise clients on political giving, and many lobbyists raise money for candidates themselves. The practice is legal, though federal law requires lobbyists to disclose their own contributions twice a year. Means also pointed to a long-running dispute about glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, which has been linked to cancer. He accused administration officials of siding with Bayer, which makes Roundup, by formally supporting the company's argument at the Supreme Court to block state lawsuits over the herbicide. A White House official told CBS News that Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote a brief at the court's request. Bayer has paid Ballard Partners since January 2024 to lobby Congress and the administration on a number of issues, according to lobbying disclosures. Ballard said no one at the firm lobbied Wiles or West Wing staff on glyphosate. Means' claim that Wiles was hostile to the MAHA agenda has drawn pushback from her allies. Two sources, who requested anonymity to describe a private meeting, recounted a White House meeting last year in which an administration official derided MAHA supporters as "nuts." Wiles shot back: "I'm one of those MAHA nuts," the sources said. A White House official told CBS News that Wiles "has been an essential leader in Making America Healthy Again." Mr. Trump's longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio, whom Means accused of working to help pharmaceutical interests, said in a statement that Means' allegation that he is "in the pocket of Big Pharma" was "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false." Fabrizio previously urged Republicans to campaign on lowering prescription drug prices, finding in an April 2025 poll that the issue could give GOP candidates in toss-up districts a 20-point boost. The fight is unlikely to fade soon. California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said he will look into the claims against Wiles. Attorney General Todd Blanche has dismissed Means as a "disgruntled former administration official," and told CNN the Justice Department would not investigate "something that someone says on a podcast." item.title: Republicans block Hegseth impeachment push, but Democrats could try again in January
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Republican-controlled U.S. House of Representatives voted on Tuesday to effectively kill the articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — for now — by blocking their consideration on the House floor and sending them back to the Judiciary Committee, where GOP leaders can hold them up until the next Congress is seated in January 2027. Democrats — who voted unanimously against shelving the impeachment charges — will have a large House majority next year after winning at least 255 seats in last week's midterm elections. They have already vowed to try to remove Hegseth from office when they take control of Congress. "In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker, said at a rally last month . Eleven Democrats missed Tuesday’s vote, which succeeded in blocking the charges by a 211 to 204 margin. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries. On Tuesday, Massie was the only Republican who broke with his party and voted to keep the articles of impeachment alive. Before Tuesday's vote, Hegseth struck a defiant tone in a Pentagon news briefing. He described the impeachment efforts as "a farce" and insisted that "none of these are high crimes or misdemeanors — they are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military." He added, "That's what it is. Policy disagreements. Not high crimes. Not misdemeanors. Not treason. Not bribery. Not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause." While Hegseth did not mention Massie by name, he criticized the actions of a "disgruntled congressman" and said the "proper remedy" for a policy disagreement was legislation. "It's a political spectacle," Hegseth said. "A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president." He added, "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage." Related: Only 2 Cabinet officials have ever been impeached. Could Pete Hegseth be next? Hegseth also said the resolution suggested the U.S. would punish its own military for carrying out its job. "Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does," he said. "It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership." President Trump celebrated Tuesday night's House vote on Truth Social , where he said that Democrats' attempt to impeach Hegseth "miserably FAILED!" Earlier in the day, Trump posted on Truth Social that Hegseth had earned an "'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" for his defense against Massie, and described the defense secretary as "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country," adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached." Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28. Pool via Getty Images The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C. , to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections . Hegseth has been facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress. "Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation." Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law." His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said. Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart." Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. It's unclear whether Massie's impeachment effort would have succeeded on the House floor under Republican control. Massie had previously told ABC News he was "confident" there would have been "enough GOP defectors for it to pass." Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor. "I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat. CBS News , however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict. The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war." The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning." "He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress." Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it." Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth." "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation . "No one's happy about Iran." A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list. Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me." item.title: Rubio says U.S. doesn't need to attack Iran again as peace talks gain momentum
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after a G7 meeting that the economic campaign against Iran meant bombing was unnecessary (Brendan SMIALOWSKI) Top US diplomat Marco Rubio said Tuesday that he saw no need to attack Iran again, as diplomatic efforts to end the war gathered steam and Tehran urged Washington to accept its demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Hours after President Donald Trump said he saw "positive momentum" towards resolving the eight-month war, Rubio said the United States' squeezing of Iran's economy made further attacks unnecessary. "The economic campaign (against Iran) is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations," the secretary of state said after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris. "That's what I told our allies here today." Iran's efforts to blockade Hormuz, the major exit route for Gulf energy shipments, have sent oil prices soaring -- a major factor in the humbling of Trump's Republicans in last week's midterm elections. Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign aimed at financially strangling Iran, already battered by years of sanctions. Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called for greater efforts to end the conflict, while warning of the economic damage of an ongoing impasse. "We need to move beyond the 'no war, no peace' stalemate, which is causing deep economic pain for our countries," he said in Paris. "We must see an all-out diplomatic effort to end this conflict, prevent a nuclear Iran and the threats it poses around the world, and get the Strait of Hormuz properly reopened." Washington has appeared to taper down its threats of renewed strikes after the Republicans' defeat, and even Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu -- who launched the war alongside Trump and recently lobbied to "forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran" -- appeared to recognise the shifting diplomatic reality. "In the very near future, we're going to be confronted by international pressure to accept a nuclear-armed Iran and the preservation of this terror regime that seeks to annihilate us," he said on Tuesday. - 'Address Iran's demands' - Tehran said its offer to reopen Hormuz within two days -- if Washington agreed to a raft of conditions -- remained on the table. Iran's demands have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing its assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US blockade of its ports. "The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the IRNA news agency. "The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran's demands and conditions -- which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table." Meanwhile, vessels continue to come under attack in and around the strait. The Emirati state oil company ADNOC said on Tuesday that one of its vessels had "sustained damage following an attack in the UAE's territorial waters", while the British maritime agency UKMTO reported a tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" off the Omani coast. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that three oil tankers were on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, though it was unclear whether they were referring to the same ships. - US 'more flexible' after midterms - On Monday, after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House, Trump said that the US was "locked and loaded", but further strikes were "quite unlikely" given that key US allies in the Gulf "would prefer the status quo". "We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected," he wrote on social media. Qatar and Pakistan are leading diplomatic efforts to resolve the war, which began with US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in late February. Qatari foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi confirmed there had been progress in the negotiations. "The mediator is making a persistent and earnest effort to bridge the gaps between the parties' positions," he told a regular briefing, adding: "We remain hopeful." Iranian political analyst Ali Bigdeli said the outcome of the US elections appeared to have "somewhat reduced Iran's flexibility, whereas the Americans have become more flexible". He noted that the Iranian terms were "demanding and heavy for the United States to accept" but added that "engaging in direct talks" could bear results. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei urged Washington to "surrender" to the Iranian demands. "The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler. Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Several members of the Kennedy family have sued President Donald Trump , aiming to stop the building of the triumphal arch he hopes to build near Washington, D.C., new court filings show. The proposed 250-foot monument in the style of Paris’ Arc de Triomphe would be built on the Virginia side of the Potomac River between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, where American veterans have been laid to rest since the Civil War. According to Kennedy family members behind the lawsuit, the 25-story arch would "cast a shadow" over memorials to their family members laid to rest in the historic burial site. "President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch," says the Kennedy family members’ lawsuit, "that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes." According to the lawsuit, the arch would block sightlines onto the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, a memorial to the former president who was assassinated in 1963 . They contend it will also cast a shadow over the graves of prominent Kennedys buried in the cemetery. In addition to JFK, others buried there include Robert F. Kennedy, the former senator assassinated in 1968 , and Sen. Edward "Ted" Kennedy, who died in 2009 after 43 years of serving in Congress. Among the nine Kennedys named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit are RFK’s daughter Kerry Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, Jr. "Vanity should never stand in the way of valor," Kerry Kennedy, president of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said in a statement following the court filing in Washington, D.C. USA TODAY has reached out to the White House and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for comment. Trump has previously promoted the project as both a landmark and a military asset. Speaking on Nov. 2 during an event highlighting improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he said the arch could house drones and snipers. "It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said. The court filing is the latest attempt to thwart the president’s attempt to build the arch. Opponents have previously argued that the arch would obstruct the view from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington Cemetery, which was built on the confiscated land of former Confederate General Robert E. Lee. The clear view between the two sites is meant to represent the reunification of the country following the Civil War, according to court filings. Plans to build Trump’s arch have been approved by a board led by people appointed by the president. But other hurdles remain. A federal judge on Nov. 5 temporarily blocked the project from going forward in response to a separate lawsuit brought by Washington and Virginia, arguing that the president needs approval from Congress in order to build. Trump's plans to remake the nation's capital, including the proposed arch, are not popular among Americans. In May, polls showed 52% of Americans were against the project, including 41% who strongly oppose it, while only 21% of people support the plan to build the towering arch. Democrats retaking Congress in the midterms argued in the run-up to the election that the president was too focused on construction projects in Washington and not focused enough on bringing down the cost of living for everyday Americans. "I don't know if you've noticed, but he is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV," former President Barack Obama quipped in one viral campaign moment. "Guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House, paved over the Rose Garden – paved it over – put a helicopter pad on the side lawn." item.title: Dreams, desks and selfies: Newly elected members of Congress learn their way around
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organizer who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-known North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,000 campaign budget, said she's excited to arrive in Washington and show what's possible. Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter said his win over incumbent GOP Rep. Max Miller ensures Ohio remains a very competitive swing state. And Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot in New Jersey who said she's spent her whole life "trying to find the biggest, hardest problem to throw myself at," was ready to give Congress a try. "There's always the unknown." They were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week for the start of freshmen orientation — the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party's sweep of the midterm elections , and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans. "People were just looking for somebody who's going to listen to them," said Womack, who said she won by simply showing up and talking with voters. "I'm a single mom and so I know what it's like to have to live on a budget and figure out how am I going to feed my family," she said. "And that's what people want to fight for them in Washington right now." New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on Jan. 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins. This week's orientation includes training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or those retiring it's the start of figuring out what's next. Briefing rooms are filled with information about office setup, payroll and benefits, and there's a room to take official portraits. It's also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House. "I'm looking forward to learning as much as I can and being the best representative I can be for my district," said Poindexter as he arrived at the nearby Navy Yard hotel where lawmakers converged. Selfies, besties and tough votes ahead The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection. President Donald Trump backed Cornyn's rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated. "I'm so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes," Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas as well. And Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews , Roy Cooper , Peggy Flanagan , Josh Turek and others. "First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn't ask for a better team," she posted as the caption. Among them was former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown , who defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted, a Trump-backed favorite, for a comeback. Brown was in the Senate for 18 years before he lost two years ago to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno, but he still joined his freshmen colleagues for their orientation. "I've actually learned some things," said Brown, who was celebrating his 74th birthday on Monday. "I've gotten to know my colleagues." Leadership elections test the new members One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they're sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership. Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices — House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer — in favor of a fresh start. Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support— the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation's first Black American to become speaker of the House. Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters' sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate . Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan announced they would not support Schumer. Sen.-elect Chris Pappas, D-N.H. — who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator — said their class is "a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington." He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him. Republicans chose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party's election defeat. Ohio Rep. Jim Jordon won the race against the No. 2 Republican Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana to become the minority leader, continuing a rivalry stretching to 2023, before Johnson rose to power. Senate Republicans tapped Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to stay on as leader, despite those agitating for a change. A diverse new class arrives As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday's session with a prayer, "some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats." On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones — Flanagan will be the first Native American female U.S. senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more. Rep. Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats' campaign chief, called the party's candidates "all very unique." "We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy award-winning musician," she said earlier. "They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp." Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol's stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men. item.title: The mysterious former journalist at the center of the Nvidia spy scandal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are seen dining at a restaurant in Shanghai. CNN geolocated the image to an upscale restaurant along Shanghai's riverfront. - From Social Media Who is Alice Huang, the woman allegedly at the center of the scandal enveloping the world’s most powerful chip company? She’s been photographed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (no relation) at banquet dinners and golf resorts, clinking wine glasses and even leaving an event with him in the same car. But for someone suddenly generating international headlines, she remains something of a mystery. Her limited online footprint paints a picture of a journalist-turned tech power broker who held senior positions at financial firms in Asia. However, US officials believe she was also working as a Chinese spy who was having an affair with the Nvidia chief – and tasked with collecting intelligence on one of the world’s most valuable tech giants in an effort to help Beijing surpass the US in AI dominance. The espionage allegations, combined with an admission of an extramarital affair by the Nvidia chief, have rocked the semiconductor behemoth and the broader chip industry. Here’s what we know about the elusive executive in the middle of it all. unknown content item - What’s her background? US Customs and Border Patrol travel records obtained by CNN that correspond with Alice Huang’s social media posts in the US identify her as a 43-year-old Chinese citizen by the name of Huang Le. According to Chinese social media and databases tracking the career of Huang Le, she worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before pivoting to a career in finance. A report from New York Times described Alice Huang as a fluent English speaker who frequented industry conferences and executive dinners, with connections at the highest levels of the AI industry. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are seen walking around an exclusive golf resort in San Martin, California. CNN geolocated the still to the luxury CordeValle resort. - From Social Media One Chinese private-equity fund website said Huang had four years of experience in the media and eight in the securities industry, including at HSBC and Citic Securities. CNN has reached out to HSBC and Citic Securities for comment. From March to November of 2023, Huang was a director at Megaspeed International, according to corporate records in Singapore, where the company is based. The cloud computing and data center provider was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Huang became director and the company changed its name, Megaspeed has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia, purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors by some analyst estimates. A screengrab from CTI video footage shows Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan on May 22, 2025. - CTI/Handout/Reuters Corporate records also indicate Megaspeed received funding from Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and the company has come under investigation for potentially providing Chinese companies with unauthorized access to US chips. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unclear - and she has made no public statement or appearance since last year, when reports of the suspicions surrounding her relationship with Jensen Huang first broke. CNN has reached out to Megaspeed, Singapore’s government and Singaporean police. How does she know Jensen Huang? It is unclear exactly where and when they met, but the Chinese executive has become something of a regular fixture in Huang’s business circles, appearing at the side of the Nvidia CEO at private and corporate events. The two were pictured together as early as September 2024 on WeChat, the ubiquitous Chinese social messaging app, at a luxury golf resort in California. Records from US Customs and Border Protection show Alice Huang has visited the US ten times since 2017. The most recent trip was in March of last year, when she was photographed visiting Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara during the company’s annual conference. In May 2025, the two attended a group dinner in Taipei during a tech conference and left in the same car. Nvidia has previously denied there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about their relationship. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said in statement from October. But on Sunday, the company said it was opening an independent investigation into whether the CEO was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The same weekend Huang admitted to his extramarital affair in a company-wide statement without naming the other party involved. Were any secrets stolen? Nvidia, which is worth about $4.5 trillion and designs some of the world’s most advanced AI chips, said as of Sunday that it has no reason to believe that state or corporate secrets had been compromised. The FBI first raised concerns to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China nearly a year ago , two people familiar with the matter told CNN. unknown content item - The New York Times also reported that intelligence officials were conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang for at least a year, and had briefed President Donald Trump on the matter last year. Trump said he did not regret not taking action, and downplayed Jensen Huang’s culpability in the incident on Monday. He said he believed that the Nvidia CEO was unaware of any potential motivations of espionage. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” CNN’s Isaac Yee and Wayne Chang contributed to this report from Taipei. item.title: Meghan Markle’s father cut off ankle monitor after child sexual abuse material arrest, DOJ says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Markle , cut off his ankle monitor while on house arrest after being charged with having child sexual abuse material, federal authorities said on Tuesday. "Four days ago, a federal judge allowed Mr. Markle to remain out of custody pending trial," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement posted to X . "He was ordered to wear a location monitoring device. He allegedly cut the bracelet off at 1:45 a.m. last night. Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions. We are asking the court to revoke his release and detain him pending trial, and we will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law." A Justice Department spokesperson told the BBC that Markle, 82, appeared in court in Tampa, Fla., on Tuesday after he allegedly removed his ankle monitor. He was reportedly ordered jailed without bond and remains in federal custody. Last Friday, Markle appeared in federal court in Tampa, hours after FBI agents arrested him at his care home. He was charged with one count of possession of child pornography. He arrived at court in a wheelchair and did not enter a plea. A magistrate judge released him on his own recognizance to home detention with electronic monitoring and barred him from traveling outside Florida's Middle District and California's Central District. The judge also ordered him to have no contact with minors and not to use devices that can access the internet, and to undergo a psychiatric evaluation before the case moved forward. According to the Justice Department, Markle was arrested after agents discovered approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books, that contained suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) while searching two storage units registered to Markle, at least one of which was in the Los Angeles area. "Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," Essayli said in a press release announcing his initial arrest. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law." In October 2026, federal law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding the discovery of suspected CSAM among Markle's possessions in the Philippines, according to the press release. Officers then interviewed a separate individual who revealed Markle had rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. This led to the discovery of a second storage unit. Both had been rented by Markle since 2008. An external view of the federal courthouse in Tampa where Thomas Markle appeared on Nov. 6. Mike Carlson via Getty Images In a statement, FBI Director Kash Patel said that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions." "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids — any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide," Patel added. If convicted, Markle could face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. "This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," said Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office. In October, it was reported that Markle was under investigation in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. Philippine authorities plan to file their own charges against him as early as Monday, ITV News reported. The Sun first reported that his son, Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., told Philippine police that after his father left the country in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu. Markle Sr. denied those allegations, telling the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick." Markle is believed to have returned to the U.S. in May, after his left leg was amputated in the Philippines in December 2025. In October, The Sun reported Markle moved into Maravida Senior Living care home, a facility which specializes in "memory care." Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, meets volunteer first responders in Bondi Beach, Australia, in April. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP Meghan Markle released a statement following the claims, saying she was "deeply distressed." She also revealed that in 2019 she received a copy of a letter containing "troubling" allegations about him, which had been sent to London's Metropolitan Police. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police subsequently said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies. According to the Sun on Sunday , Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case. Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them." She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her. item.title: D.C.'s youngest-ever lawmaker just took office. He could be out in days.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The youngest D.C. lawmaker ever and the first to belong to Generation Z was sworn in to the D.C. Council on Monday before a packed council chamber of supporters. But the milestone may be short-lived. The new at-large council member, 28-year-old Jamal Holtz, the president of D.C. Young Democrats, may only last a few weeks or days in the job, which he accepted after a political chess match over the seat. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. After a week of political turmoil, Holtz was appointed by the D.C. Democratic Party to temporarily fill the at-large council seat vacated by Del.-elect Robert C. White Jr. (D). Holtz said he did not ask for the position. And the party made clear it only intended Holtz as a placeholder, announced in a rush last week to block another council member from claiming it. Holtz said he has not applied for the job and doesn't intend to. That means a different person could be appointed by the Democratic Party as interim council member as soon as it completes a more formal interview process. The saga will not end there. There will also be a special election for the seat on April 6, making it possible a new person, again, will claim the seat. Even Holtz himself acknowledged the circumstances of his appointment were highly unusual, joking that they were reminiscent of "a sixth season of 'House of Cards,'" the Netflix political thriller. But he said he would give to the role the "seriousness, the energy and the commitment" that residents deserved no matter how long he served. "Because whether you serve for one day or for one decade, the responsibility of public service does not change ," he said. In a speech before the packed council chamber, Holtz said he would bring his lived experiences as a fourth-generation Washingtonian into the job to advocate for the needs of D.C. residents. He knows what it's like to lose a brother to gun violence, he said. To be homeless and spend days living out of a car, and to watch his mother and others in his life struggle to put food on the table. "Now I have an opportunity to give back to the city that bought into me ," he said. The chaotic process surrounding Holtz's appointment kicked off after White's resignation from the D.C. Council last week. Immediately afterward, council member Christina Henderson (I-At Large) attempted to switch her party affiliation to Democrat to slide into the seat, allowing her to rejoin the party ahead of a consequential presidential election and to eventually seek higher office within the city's dominant political party. But from the vantage point of party faithful, her move was an attempt to "usurp" the party's nomination process as laid out in the D.C. Home Rule Act. D.C.'s home rule charter caps the number of Democrats who can serve on the council, and Henderson's party switch would have hit the limit. But Henderson stood down on Friday, switching back to independent and clearing the way for Holtz's appointment. D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson (D) told reporters ahead of the ceremony that he didn't disagree that the process was "confusing and certainly unprecedented." But he said he did not feel he could second-guess the Democratic Party's process and that he had "no choice" but to move ahead with Holtz and, possibly, with a new person if the party goes that route. At least one former council member, Jack Evans, the former finance committee chairman who spent three decades on the council until his resignation in 2020 amid an ethics probe, said he is applying through the Democratic Party's process and planning to run in the special election. Chioma Iwuoha, chair of the D.C. Democratic Party, told reporters the party would be meeting again this week to chart its next steps. She did not yet have an exact timeline for a final vote on a potential new appointee. Asked if Holtz would be considered, she said he had committed to not seeking the role but added: "He has the right to change his mind."
